New AJK government’s task. DESPITE hurdles, doubts, speculation, a protest movement and delayed polls on seven out of 45 directly contested Legislative Assembly seats, the task of installing a new government in Azad Jammu and Kashmir has finally been accomplished. There had been serious questions about the fairness of the elections. The bitterest criticism was from the PPP, the PML-N’s ally in the national parliament. Even the AJK prime minister’s election was not without controversy. Barrister Iftikhar Gillani was not selected or even recommended as a candidate for the office by the PML-N parliamentary party of the AJK assembly; rather, he was picked by the president of PML-N Pakistan. The choice was resented by some senior party leaders, including Shah Ghulam Qadir, the party president in AJK, who boycotted the assembly session that elected the PM. The key objection to Mr Gillani’s election as PM was not his relative inexperience compared to veterans such as former PM Raja Farooq Haider or former speaker Shah Ghulam Qadir but the mode of his election as an assembly member. He had lost his seat — the Muzaffarabad constituency, LA-29 — to his PPP rival in the election by over 3,000 votes. Still, he returned to the assembly on a seat reserved for technocrats. There is no legal bar to the eligibility of a member who is defeated in the general election and subsequently elected on a reserved seat to seek the PM’s office. But many politicians believe that a PM should win the confidence of his constituency before seeking the coveted position. However, despite a turbulent electoral phase that had been ongoing for some months, the new government and PM have assumed office in AJK. Given the PML-N’s clear majority in the assembly, the election of a new AJK president of the PML-N’s choice will likely be a formality. The most important question, however, concerns the new government’s agenda and how far it can overcome the most serious challenges ever faced by an AJK government. A negotiated solution must be found for all contentious issues. In view of the circumstances surrounding the entire electoral process, the foremost challenge before the new government and the PM is to establish the government’s moral and performance legitimacy, even if one accepts its electoral legitimacy. Opening the lines of communication with the outlawed Joint Awami Action Committee, engaging with the saner elements within the organisation, and convincing them to abandon the agitation will be the government’s first major test. If successful, it will pave the way for legitimacy of performance. Although the outlawed JAAC can justifiably be blamed for several irresponsible and anti-state utterances and actions, the fact remains that the defunct organisation has a sizeable following, especially in Poonch division, where, despite its best efforts, including organising phased polls, the AJK Election Commission could not hold elections in seven out of 11 constituencies. A sizeable crowd has been staging a sit-in for almost three months, partly paralysing civic life and links with the rest of AJK and Pakistan. The confrontation and deaths of some agitators and law-enforcement personnel have polarised Kashmiris not only in AJK but also among the diaspora. This confrontation has damaged goodwill and the moral standing of authorities in AJK and Pakistan. The situation, therefore, must be defused immediately and a negotiated solution found for the contentious issues. It was unreasonable, arguably, for the outlawed JAAC to insist on immediately abolishing the 12 AJK assembly seats reserved for Kashmiri refugees settled in various parts of Pakistan. This demand became even more absurd after the AJK Supreme Court ruled in June that the legislative assembly seats reserved for refugees were constitutionally protected and could not be abolished through executive action or street protests. However, it is also true that the constitutional reforms on the allocation of seats between refugees from the occupied Kashmir valley and Jammu need to be seriously considered, along with the election procedure. The election to the AJK assembly from various parts of Pakistan is generally heavily influenced by the federal and provincial governments during the poll cycle. Now that the new legislative assembly is in place, it should seriously initiate deliberations on constitutional reforms. In general, the outlawed JAAC’s demands are not unreasonable and are mostly directed at welfare measures and better governance. For example, the demand for a smaller cabinet and the abolition of lavish facilities for elected representatives and senior bureaucrats should be sympathetically considered, alongside calls for roads, tunnels, bridges, safe drinking water, and preventing development budgetary funds from lapsing. Demanding empowered local governments and elected students’ unions is also fair. These are not just JAAC demands, but what every Kashmiri and also many in Pakistan demand. The new government can build on the previous government’s acceptance of most demands and begin implementing the points already agreed upon. The new PM may begin by forming a smaller cabinet and cutting back on unnecessary protocol and unproductive spending. If tangible steps are taken early for better governance, a solid foundation may be laid for broader reconciliation. In the long term, both the federal government in Pakistan and the AJK government should consider granting AJK the same rights and privileges enjoyed by the four provinces. The same goes for Gilgit-Baltistan. A constitutional way should be found to provide interim representation to AJK and GB in federal institutions such as parliament, the Council of Common Interests, the National Economic Council and the water regulator Irsa, without compromising our position on the Kashmir dispute. The denial of these rights over the last 80 years has become a major source of grievance. The writer is president of the Pakistan-based think tank Pildat. president@pildat.org X: @ABMPildat Published in Dawn, September 5th, 2026

Shame and shamelessness. “You must never lose your sense of shame. If one is past all shame, what is one fit for? One lives like a bird in moult, shedding virtues like plumes all pointing down to hell” — Wolfram von Eschenbach (German poet.) I’VE been wrestling with this idea — the essentiality of shame for retaining humanity — for some time now. But I am reminded of it every time I read in the news about how one judge or the other has, again, successfully continued Imaan Mazari and Hadi Chattha’s perverse incarceration . The novel Shame presents another take on the idea. While acknowledging its necessity, it argues shame is never truly lost. It is suppressed, it is unacknowledged, it is transferred to others, but it invariably re-emerges, nay erupts, mutated into manifestations of violence and tyranny throughout society. Surviving in Pakistan (but, more specifically, thriving in Pakistan) demands the suppression of shame. Being more fortunate, we suppress the shame of a cruel and rapacious system built to profit the powerful by exploiting the powerless. As Muslims, we suppress our shame at how we steadily criminalise the very existence of our minorities and force them to leap through ever-higher hoops to earn their right to live. As citizens, we suppress the shame of a state that has long abandoned any pretence to being representative and casually disappears dissidents. As lawyers, we suppress the shame of a legal system indifferent to justice and riddled with cowardice and venality. We suppress the shame, not only from fear of the consequences of speaking or acting, but so we can live with ourselves. There are a few, however, who feel the sting of shame more sharply. They speak, and act, while we watch. They carry the burden of our collective shame and expiate it. There are a few who carry the burden of our collective shame and expiate it. Imaan and Hadi belong on that list. One might not subscribe to all their opinions. One might think them misguided in some of the causes they choose to advocate. And, while ensconced in the quiet safety of one’s living room, one can disagree with their or, more particularly, her manner of articulation. But while we may not possess the courage to emulate them, do we lack even the shame to admire them? This January, Judge Afzal Manjoka sentenced the couple to prison for 17 years. As per the judgement, Imaan’s crime was sending six tweets. In one, she posted a picture of Mahrang Baloch raising a victory sign and encouraged the public to raise their voice against fake encounters, enforced disappearances and killings in Balochistan. In another, she said innocents kept in illegal detention and torture cells were also victims — just like those targeted in terrorist attacks. In a third tweet, she said state repression in Balochistan was making the insurgency worse. In a fourth, she argued that reports about anti-terrorist operations by security officials in Balochistan had lost credibility. Two of her tweets were about KP. In the first, she said “we said never forget but acted like nothing happened. The terrorist who had our children slaughtered was set free by the state. The disastrous good Taliban vs bad Taliban policy continues even today”. Presumably, she was referring to the TTP’s former spokesperson, Ehsanullah Ehsan, who initially surrendered and was detained in a military safe-house but later ‘escaped’ and claimed to be living the expatriate’s dream in Turkiye. Notably, the parents of the 147 children in the Army Public School massacre earlier raised the same grievance in their petition before the Supreme Court. Her second tweet condemned the forced disappearance of Ghazi Amanullah, brother of PTM leader Manzoor Pashteen, and argued the state was targeting peaceful dissidents and their families. As I said earlier, one might object to the tenor of some of her speech. But the content? Who seriously disagrees that the good Taliban, bad Taliban strategy we’ve followed on and off in Afghanistan and Pakistan for three decades has, on each occasion, come back to bite us? Or that decades of the state’s undiscriminating repression in Balochistan has only fuelled the insurgency? But even if you disagree, and are a genuine adherent of the ‘Pindi knows best’ philosophy, do you reckon people expressing the contrary view should be convicted of terrorism and jailed for 17 years? Poor Hadi, of course, didn’t even tweet anything himself. The judgement accuses him, however, of retweeting four of Imaan’s tweets. Unstated in the judgement (but imprudently expressed by Chief Justice Sarfaraz Dogar in an earlier, unrelated, case) is his true crime: being a Pakistani man who cannot control his own wife. But my question is not to Judge Manjoka, nor about how closely his judgement of Jan 24 hews to the narrative expressed in the press conference held on Jan 6 by a security official accusing Imaan of being “a lawyer for terrorists” and “a foreign agent”. My question is to everyone who wears a judicial robe: how is it possible to witness the travesty of Imaan and Hadi’s trial, the breach of every principle of due process, the utter frivolity of the charges against them, the draconian punishments awarded to them, and not feel an outpouring of shame at one’s own helplessness? It is to everyone who wears a black coat. How can one belong to a profession committed to upholding the rule of law yet observe the presidents of the Supreme Court Bar and Islamabad High Court Bar (belonging to the Asma Jahangir group, no less!) defending these convictions; and witness the failure of the majority of bars to rise to the defence of their own, without feeling the sharp sting of shame? The question is about the nature of shame itself. What happens to a society forced to live without it? The writer is a member of the Pakistan Bar Council. Published in Dawn, September 5th, 2026

Bond revival. PAKISTAN has raised a record $3bn in its single largest international capital market transaction through a dual-tranche Eurobond sale that drew nearly $6bn in total orders. When international investors offer to lend a country almost twice what it is asking for and are willing to do so for as long as 10 years, they are betting that Pakistan will still be solvent, still servicing its debt, and still worth holding paper on a decade from now. That bet placed by a widespread group of institutional buyers gives yet another positive spin to the economic revival story told by the government. Two years after the country was on the verge of default, that is no mean achievement. Some practical gains from this stand out: a boost to reserves, a fresh pricing benchmark, and less reliance on bilateral rollovers. Locking in money for 5.5 and 10 years, rather than the shorter rollovers that have dominated Pakistan’s external financing in recent years, pushes out the point at which this debt has to be refinanced. Following recent rating upgrades , this is the kind of market validation the country needed. None of that should be mistaken for cheap money, though. The coupon rates — almost equal to returns the government is paying on Roshan Digital deposits — are real, high rates in a hard currency Pakistan cannot print and is struggling to earn. For context, when Islamabad last issued dollar bonds in 2021, it borrowed five-year money at 5.875pc and 10-year money at 7.375pc. In other words, this deal costs more than the last comparable one did. Part of that gap can be attributed to international factors: global dollar rates have stayed higher for longer since the Fed’s tightening cycle, so every sovereign borrower, not just Pakistan, is paying more than it would have three or four years ago. But part of it is also Pakistan-specific. Investors are still charging a risk premium that an investment-grade country would not pay. That does not mean Pakistan has borrowed badly. It is just that the current ratings can only do so much in the prevailing market. Comparing Eurobond coupons across countries can be tricky because a rate that looks high for one issuer can be a bargain for another, once credit rating, tenor and the global rate environment are accounted for. Judged against peers of similar credit standing, Pakistan’s pricing sits towards the upper end of the range, which aligns with where the rating agencies currently place it: not investment grade, but no longer treated as a basket case either. The more useful test of this deal will come later: whether Pakistan can return to the market in a year or two and borrow at a lower cost than it did with this issue will be the real test. It will determine if the confidence on display is durable. Published in Dawn, September 5th, 2026

Asif says devolution of power is 'inevitable', accuses PPP of having contradictory stance on new provinces. Defence Minister Khawaja Asif has said that the devolution of power is “inevitable”, while also accusing the PPP of having a contradictory stance on the issue of new provinces. “When there is talk of a Saraiki province in Punjab, the PPP supports it or shows a soft corner on this issue. And when there is talk of multiple provinces or administrative units instead of four, talk of ‘Sindhudesh’ begins,” he said in a post on the social media platform X late Saturday night. On Friday, the Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan (MQM-P) was denied the opportunity to present a resolution against the “Sindhudesh movement”. The PPP had slammed the party for attempting to “mislead the people” by tabling the resolution. Asif said that he saw “something else” behind this “dual policy” by the PPP, adding that he would delve into this deeper “when the time comes”. “We are first and foremost Pakistanis. Devolution was decided as a constitutional principle through the 18th Amendment, which was not respected. Time and circumstance demand that it be implemented with integrity,” he said. He said that concentration of power had made the current system obsolete, which needed to be “corrected”. “Provinces or administrative units, whatever label you want to apply. You have 36 divisions, use them, or devise some other administrative-geographical scheme. The devolution of power is inevitable,” he said. Asif’s remarks come as the PPP, a key ally of the PML-N-led ruling coalition, has questioned Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s silence over the debate on creating new provinces and sought his stance on the matter. The PPP had earlier maintained that any move to create additional federating units must follow the procedure laid down in the Constitution. However, the PPP-led Sindh government on Wednesday got a resolution passed by the provincial assembly opposing any further division of the country’s existing four provinces. A debate over the creation of new federating units has continued for the past couple of months in different circles, although there has been no official confirmation about the origin or contours of any proposal. However, some ruling-party leaders and federal cabinet members have publicly expressed support for the idea at different forums, including parliament. Media reports have suggested proposals ranging from eight to as many as 30 provinces, though no official plan has been announced. Talking to Dawn on Friday, PPP Parliamentarians Secretary General Nayyar Hussain Bokhari sought the prime minister’s position on the issue. Bokhari said that if the government was serious about increasing the number of provinces, it should first bring the matter before the federal cabinet, after which the prime minister should take all stakeholders and political parties on board. He recalled that consultations between the government and political parties had continued for months during the framing of the 1973 Constitution, while deliberations preceding the 18th Constitutional Amendment had lasted for more than a year. Bokhari, who also raised the issue during a talk show on DawnNewsTV on Friday, said the consent of the provinces was essential for carving out new federating units. He said any such move would also require the necessary constitutional amendment to be passed by both the National Assembly and Senate with a two-thirds majority. The PML-N-led government enjoys a two-thirds majority in the National Assembly with the PPP’s support. Therefore, if the PPP pulled back its support, it would become impossible for the government to implement the idea. Responding to a question about the local government system in the country, Bokhari said any move in that regard must also follow the Constitution, particularly Article 140-A, which provides for the establishment of local governments by the provinces. Meanwhile, PML-N leader and Adviser to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah on Friday reiterated that no preparations were currently under way for the creation of new provinces. Sanaullah told a private television channel that no bill or resolution regarding the creation of new provinces had been presented in parliament. He said consultation and consensus among political parties would be essential before any such bill or resolution could be brought before parliament. Responding to a question, he said there was currently no discussion under way regarding the division of the existing provinces.

Skardu by-election: Polling underway at 61 polling stations amid tight security. GILGIT: Polling is currently underway at 61 polling stations in the GBA-09 (Skardu-III) constituency amid tight security. The process began at 8am and will continue till 5pm. State broadcaster PTV said 33,985 voters would exercise their right to franchise, adding that special security arrangement had been made for the occasion. The by-election was announced by the Gilgit-Baltistan Election Commission after the GB Supreme Appellate Court disqualified PPP candidate Fida Muhammad Nashad, who had been declared a returned candidate in the June general elections . Nashad’s son, Akhtar Abbas, is contesting the election on PPP’s ticket, while Mohammad Ajmal is contesting from the PML-N. Former minister Mohammad Saleem, who is contesting as an independent, is also among 10 candidates who have filed their nomination papers. Analysts said a close contest was expected between PPP’s Abbas and independent candidate Saleem. They said Abbas could retain his father’s vote bank and may benefit from public sympathy following Nashad’s disqualification by the GB Supreme Appellate Court. District Returning Officer (DRO) Hamza Murad told Dawn on Friday that GBA-09 had 61 polling stations, of which 25 had been declared sensitive under Category A, 11 had been placed in Category B as medium-sensitive, and 25 had been classified as normal under Category C.

Bolivian army base blasts kill 2, wound dozens. Two explosions at an army barracks in Bolivia killed at least two people and wounded 81 on Friday, authorities said. Defence Minister Ernesto Justiniano said “pyrotechnic material” was stored at the base in Viacha, southwest of Bolivia’s administrative capital La Paz. The exact cause of the blasts, which happened at around 2:30pm (1830 GMT), was under investigation, he said in a statement. Footage circulated by local media showed a thick column of black smoke rising from the city center. Houses in the area were damaged by the blasts, with footage showing shattered windows, broken ceilings and scattered debris. Justiniano said two people were confirmed dead and seven people were missing. The wounded, including two people in “serious condition,” were taken to medical centres, he added. Chad Blames Sudan’s Army for Strikes on Convoy cmoore Fri, 08/28/2026 - 12:46 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Analyst's Notebook / Africa 28 August 2026 2 minutes Chad Blames Sudan’s Army for Strikes on Convoy Crisis Group expert Fulbert Ngodji sheds light on an air raid in Chad that is believed to have destroyed trucks carrying supplies for one of the main belligerents in the Sudanese civil war. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Fulbert Ngodji Analyst, Central Africa https://www.linkedin.com/in/fulbert-dg-ngodji-459054147/ Related Tags Chad Sudan On 22 August, the Chadian army accused its Sudanese counterpart of attacking a convoy in eastern Chad. In a televised statement , the army spokesman said Sudanese army aircraft and drones had pursued the trucks over 100km into Chad two days earlier before striking them in Mourdi department, Ennedi-Est province. Pro-Sudanese army online platforms circulated images purporting to show the army disabling several vehicles carrying supplies for the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the paramilitary group it has been fighting for control of Sudan since April 2023. The Sudanese army has not directly responded to the allegation, merely affirming its “respect for Chad’s sovereignty” in a 27 August statement . Open-source data and confidential sources have allowed Crisis Group to piece together a plausible account of what happened. A convoy of around 200 military pickup trucks reportedly left Libya and crossed Chad en route to Sudan. The Sudanese army or one of its allies then appears to have attacked the trucks near the Chadian border, as part of a months-long aerial campaign to disrupt RSF supply lines from Libya. About 70 vehicles tried to escape by crossing back into Chad, where they were destroyed. Satellite imagery showing smoke rising from the area seems to corroborate the Chadian army’s charge. It is unclear, however, who was driving the trucks and what they were carrying. The Chadian army did not address these questions. The conflict in Sudan has repeatedly spilled into Chad, primarily through an influx of refugees and, more recently, cross-border violence. Since December 2025, Chad’s eastern border has seen at least eleven incursions and drone strikes, which reportedly have killed about 30 civilians and soldiers. N’Djamena has typically sent military reinforcements or closed the border in response, but to this point it had refrained from blaming either of the main warring parties in Sudan. The 22 August statement is a departure from the previous caution, raising concerns that Chad will be drawn deeper into the civil war next door. Not only could Chad’s allegation sharpen tensions with the army-aligned authorities in Khartoum, but it could also reinforce perceptions that N’djamena has chosen sides in Sudan’s war, indirectly supporting the RSF. These perceptions are based on evidence that the United Arab Emirates has been using Chadian territory to provide the RSF with weapons and equipment. N’Djamena and Abu Dhabi have consistently denied these claims. Even so, escalation is unlikely: a confrontation would be costly for both N’Djamena and the Sudanese army. President Mahamat Déby is struggling to contain anger among his Zaghawa ethnic group, which has dominated Chad’s ruling elite since 1990. Many Zaghawa resent the government’s alleged backing of the RSF. The Sudanese army, meanwhile, controls Khartoum and much of central, northern and eastern Sudan, but remains locked in a war of attrition with no end in sight. Still, if the Sudanese army did in fact conduct the strike, its scale sets a dangerous precedent and could pave the way for more attacks by Sudanese belligerents, fuelling risks of a response by N’Djamena.
